items.why: The negation cleanly targets changing his ways, though the answer is easily lifted from the opening clause.
The question's multiple pronouns and vague “gives” blur original declarer with current speaker.
It cleanly contrasts the group credited with four victories against Jonathan's single victory.
The fulfilled prediction clearly resolves the trampled person as the officer, not the speaker.
The subject shift from the sons who saddle the donkey to the prophet who mounts it is clear.
“First” decisively distinguishes the three-party covenant from the immediately following two-party covenant.
The chronology clearly places Jotham's succession after the burial and Isaiah's record earlier.
The explicit because-clause distinguishes Uzziah's affliction from the priests' preceding action.
The embedded plan clearly places entering the city after capturing the people.
The chosen surrender plan is clearly distinguished from the rejected hypothetical of entering the city.
The order of the two Gob battles identifies Sibbekai, though the task is simple sequencing.
“What is later reported?” is vague, and reporting a camp is not a plausible competing event.
The pronoun points to the man of God, but the king ordering his own capture is implausible.
The follower relation is clear, but naming Azariah as whom his own group follows is self-defeating.
The possessive roles must be mapped across today and tomorrow to identify the other woman's child.
The relative clause directly makes Zechariah the instructor, while Amaziah is only a model.
The reply after the officer's doubt is sharply distinguished from Elisha's earlier price prophecy.
The command explicitly motivates the refusal, but treating half the kingdom as insufficient is not credible.
The event sequence clearly places continued talking immediately before Paul's departure.
Mobilizing the army plainly precedes marching and laying siege in the stated sequence.
The passage cleanly separates Jehoiada as giver from David as the weapons' former owner.
The command explicitly targets the accusers, while the Sanhedrin is only the earlier venue.
Making Uzziah king is the stated purpose, though Amaziah's death is also a reasonable background cause.
“Under their command” clearly links the army to the 2,600 leaders rather than its musterers.
The shifting pronouns require correctly tracking the man of God after the prophet saddles the donkey.
The officer's gate assignment supplies the clear antecedent of the person trampled there.
The complex duty assignments specifically give the two off-duty companies the temple-protection role.
The letter heading cleanly distinguishes Claudius Lysias as sender from Felix as addressee.
Abishai's rescue of David makes the struck victim Ishbi-Benob, not the person rescued.
The new plan to report immediately is clearly separated from the men's earlier hiding of goods.
Within Paul's quoted instruction, the young man is the one carrying information to the commander.
The messengers' return and report directly precede the people's plundering of the camp.
The singular pronoun identifies Uzziah, making the plural workers an easy grammatical rejection.
The speaker's “my son” fixes which child was eaten before the other child was hidden.
The requester and the person who intercedes are explicitly distinct participants.
The three opponents aided against are clearly listed before the unrelated Ammonite tribute.
The prophet first brings the body to his city and only afterward lays it in his tomb.
Joash is the hidden son, whereas Ahaziah has already been identified as dead.
The because-clause explicitly attributes the city's calm to Athaliah's death, not the rejoicing.
The two centurions receive the order; the soldiers are personnel they must prepare.
The Arameans distinguish the hired Hittite and Egyptian attackers from the hiring Israelite king.
The murderer is the messenger's master who sent him, cleanly identifying the king.
The quoted “him” refers to the man of God being brought back to eat and drink.
The departure plan explicitly explains the long speech, but the lamps are not a plausible cause.
The contrast between cavalry continuing and the other soldiers returning resolves the group reference precisely.
The possessed man administers the beating, while the seven sons are the ones who flee.
The wording is awkward and the answer can be found by matching the single verb “left.”
The Sanhedrin is to petition the commander, who is the one expected to bring Paul.
Burning immediately follows gathering the scrolls, while valuation is mentioned afterward.
The explicit sword clause targets followers, but the woman is also ordered out and then executed, creating ambiguity.
Hearing the noise causes Athaliah to go; seeing the king happens only after she arrives.
Consent is the stated trigger, but the broad word “act” leaves the intended moment underspecified.
The warning is addressed to the man of God, sharply separating his body from the prophet speaker.
The prophecy assigns the future sacrifice to Josiah, while Jeroboam merely stands at the altar.
